We present a new methodology for proving distribution testing lower bounds, establishing a connection between distribution testing and the simultaneous message passing (SMP) communication model. Extending the framework of Blais, Brody, and Matulef [15], we show a simple way to reduce (private-coin) SMP problems to distribution testing problems. This method allows us to prove new distribution testing lower bounds, as well as to provide simple proofs of known lower bounds.
          
            Our main result is concerned with testing identity to a specific distribution,
            p
            , given as a parameter. In a recent and influential work, Valiant and Valiant [55] showed that the sample complexity of the aforementioned problem is closely related to the ℓ
            2/3
            -quasinorm of
            p
            . We obtain alternative bounds on the complexity of this problem in terms of an arguably more intuitive measure and using simpler proofs. More specifically, we prove that the sample complexity is essentially determined by a fundamental operator in the theory of interpolation of Banach spaces, known as Peetre’s
            K-functional
            . We show that this quantity is closely related to the size of the effective support of
            p
            (loosely speaking, the number of supported elements that constitute the vast majority of the mass of
            p
            ). This result, in turn, stems from an unexpected connection to functional analysis and refined concentration of measure inequalities, which arise naturally in our reduction.

result.paraphrase:
We introduce a new approach to proving lower bounds for distribution testing by linking distribution testing with the simultaneous message passing (SMP) communication model. Building on the framework of Blais, Brody, and Matulef [15], we give a straightforward reduction from private-coin SMP problems to distribution testing tasks. This yields new lower bounds for distribution testing and also simplified proofs of previously known ones.

Our main theorem addresses testing whether a distribution is identical to a specified distribution p, where p is part of the input. In a recent influential paper, Valiant and Valiant [55] showed that the sample complexity of this problem is tightly connected to the ℓ2/3-quasinorm of p. We derive alternative complexity bounds in terms of a more intuitive quantity, with simpler arguments. In particular, we prove that the sample complexity is essentially governed by a basic operator from Banach space interpolation theory, Peetre’s K-functional. We then show that this operator is closely tied to the effective support size of p, meaning roughly the number of support points carrying most of p’s mass. This follows from an unexpected link to functional analysis and sharper concentration-of-measure inequalities that emerge naturally from our reduction.
